objects.notes: Clauses 5.1 General and 5.10 Recording and reporting establish the structured, documented approach to AI impact assessment — directly implements GOVERN 1 policies and practices for mapping, measuring, and managing AI risks.

Clause 5.6 Allocating responsibilities and 5.11 Approval process establish accountability structures for AI impact assessment — implements GOVERN 2 empowering appropriate teams and individuals for managing AI risks.

Clause 5.4 Timing and 5.6 Allocating responsibilities support GOVERN 4 — organisational teams committed to a culture that considers and communicates AI risk through systematic impact assessment practices.
Clause 5.5 Scope of the AI system impact assessment supports MAP 2 — categorisation of the AI system requires understanding its technical characteristics, data, and deployment context.

Clauses 5.7 Thresholds and 5.8 Performing the assessment provide the methodology for evaluating AI systems for trustworthiness characteristics — directly implements MEASURE 2 evaluation for robustness, fairness, and safety.
Clauses 5.10 Recording and 5.12 Monitoring and review ensure assessment outcomes are documented and continuously updated — supports GOVERN 1 transparency and effective management of AI risks.

Clause 5.11 Approval process formalises accountability for assessment outcomes — supports GOVERN 2 accountability structures ensuring responsible individuals are empowered to act on assessment results.
Clauses 5.9 Analysing results and 5.12 Monitoring and review provide mechanisms for tracking identified AI risks over time — directly implements MEASURE 3 risk tracking mechanisms.
Clauses 5.9 and 5.12 gather and assess feedback on the efficacy of impact assessment — implements MEASURE 4 feedback about the effectiveness of measurement and risk management.

Clauses 6.2 Scope, 6.3 AI system information (purpose, intended/unintended uses), 6.6 Deployment environment, and 6.7 Interested parties collectively establish the AI system context — the core of MAP 1.
Clauses 6.2 Scope, 6.3.1 AI system description, and 6.3.2 Functionalities support MAP 2 categorisation — understanding the technical nature of the AI system for proper risk classification.

Clause 6.3 AI system information (description, functionalities, purpose, intended uses) provides the system characterisation needed for MAP 3 — understanding AI capabilities, targeted usage, and expected benefits and costs.

Clauses 6.4 Data information and quality and 6.5 Algorithm and model information document the technical basis of the AI system — essential for MAP 2 AI system categorisation and scientific integrity assessment.
Clause 6.7 Relevant interested parties (directly affected and other stakeholders) implements GOVERN 5 — processes for robust engagement with relevant AI actors in the impact assessment process.

Clauses 6.6.1 Geographical area and languages and 6.6.2 Deployment environment complexity provide the deployment context essential for MAP 1 context establishment — understanding the specific settings of AI system use.

Clauses 6.8.1 General, 6.8.2 Benefits and harms, and 6.8.3 AI system failures and foreseeable misuse characterise the full impact landscape — directly implements MAP 5 impact characterisation for individuals, groups, and society.

Clause 6.8 Actual and reasonably foreseeable impacts — including failure modes and misuse scenarios — provides the trustworthiness evaluation data required by MEASURE 2 for evaluating AI systems against defined criteria.

A structured, documented impact assessment process with monitoring and review (5.1, 5.10, 5.12) is a core accountability mechanism — implements OECD Principle 5 accountability for the proper functioning of AI systems.

Integrating impact assessment with AI management and risk management processes (5.3), establishing timing across the lifecycle (5.4), and allocating responsibilities (5.6) support OECD Principle 4 lifecycle robustness and safety.

Establishing thresholds for sensitive and restricted uses (5.7) and performing the assessment (5.8) ensures human impacts, rights, and fairness considerations are evaluated — implements OECD Principle 2 human-centred values.

Analysis, recording, approval, and monitoring of impact assessment outcomes (5.9-5.12) constitute the accountability trail required by OECD Principle 5 — enabling traceability and auditability of AI impact decisions.

Documentation of assessment scope, AI system description, functionalities, and intended/unintended uses (6.2-6.3) provides the meaningful information about AI systems required by OECD Principle 3 transparency.

Identifying actual and reasonably foreseeable benefits and harms to individuals, groups, and society (6.8-6.9) is the primary instrument for implementing OECD Principle 1 — ensuring AI drives inclusive growth and does not cause societal harm.

Clauses 5.1 General and 5.2 Purpose establish the structured, documented AI impact assessment process — directly implements the QMS documentation and governance requirements of Art. 17 which mandates a formal quality management system for high-risk AI.

Clause 5.3 Integration with AI management system aligns the impact assessment with the broader AI governance system — supporting Art. 17 QMS requirements for integrated risk and quality management in high-risk AI systems.

Clause 5.3 Integration with risk management ensures impact assessment is embedded in the Art. 9 risk management system — ISO 42005 assessment methodology operationalises the Art. 9 risk management obligations when integrated with the AIMS.

Clause 5.7 Thresholds for sensitive and restricted uses, and 5.8 Performing the assessment, identify risks through structured assessment methodology — directly implements Art. 9(2) risk identification requirements for high-risk AI systems.

Clause 5.8 Performing the assessment against established thresholds evaluates likelihood and severity of identified AI impacts — implementing Art. 9(4) risk estimation and evaluation for the purposes of EU AI Act compliance.

Clauses 5.9 Analysing results and 5.11 Approval process generate the documented impact analysis required for Art. 27 Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment — ISO 42005 assessment outputs are the primary evidence artefact for FRIA compliance.

Clauses 5.10 Recording and reporting produce documented assessment outputs that form part of the technical file — Art. 11 technical documentation requirements include impact assessment records as evidence of conformity with risk management obligations.

Clauses 6.2 Scope, 6.3 AI system information, and 6.5 Algorithm and model information document the AI system in detail — this documentation directly satisfies Art. 11 technical documentation requirements for system description, capabilities, and limitations.

Clauses 6.3 AI system information (description, intended uses) and 6.7 Interested parties provide the information deployers and users require — directly supporting Art. 13 transparency obligations requiring providers to supply clear information to deployers.

Clause 6.6 Deployment environment (6.6.1 Geographical area, 6.6.2 Deployment complexity) establishes the context that deployers operate in — informing Art. 26 deployer obligations including oversight measures appropriate to the specific deployment environment.

Clauses 6.8.1 General, 6.8.2 Benefits and harms, and 6.9 Comparing and prioritising impacts constitute the full impact identification methodology — the primary operational instrument for performing the Art. 27 Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment required for high-risk AI deployers.

ISO 42005 Clauses 5.1 General and 5.2 Purpose define the structured impact assessment process that operationalises the ISO 42001 A.5.2-5 impact assessment obligation — ISO 42005 is the detailed methodological implementation of the requirement mandated by ISO 42001 A.5.

ISO 42005 Clause 5.3 Integration with AI management, risk management, and other assessment processes embeds the impact assessment within the broader AIMS — directly implementing ISO 42001 A.5.2 integration requirement for the impact assessment process.

ISO 42005 Clause 5.4 Timing of impact assessment requires assessment during the development lifecycle — this integrates with ISO 42001 A.6.1 AI development governance, ensuring impact assessment is a gate in the development approval process.

ISO 42005 Clauses 5.7 Thresholds and 5.8 Performing the assessment provide the detailed assessment methodology — the operational implementation of ISO 42001 A.5.2-5 impact assessment requirements, specifying how to conduct the assessment mandated by A.5.

ISO 42005 Clauses 5.9 Analysing results, 5.10 Recording, 5.11 Approval, and 5.12 Monitoring complete the impact assessment cycle — implementing the full documentation and monitoring requirements of ISO 42001 A.5.4-5.5 post-assessment obligations.

ISO 42005 Clause 6.2 Scope and 6.3 AI system information require detailed characterisation of the AI system being assessed — this information is generated by and must be consistent with ISO 42001 A.6.1 AI development governance documentation (design specs, intended use, approval records).

ISO 42005 Clauses 6.4 Data information and quality and 6.5 Algorithm and model information require documentation of training data, quality criteria, and algorithmic characteristics — this data documentation directly extends ISO 42001 A.7.2-6 data governance requirements to the impact assessment context.

ISO 42005 Clause 6.6 Deployment environment establishes the context in which human oversight must operate — the deployment environment characterisation informs ISO 42001 A.9.2-4 responsible use obligations and the appropriate design of human oversight mechanisms.

ISO 42005 Clauses 6.8 Actual and reasonably foreseeable impacts (6.8.2 Benefits and harms, 6.8.3 Failures and misuse, 6.9 Comparing impacts) contain the core impact identification methodology — the operational heart of ISO 42001 A.5.2-5 impact assessment execution.

ISO 42005 Clause 6.8.3 AI system failures and reasonably foreseeable misuse scenarios identify use-case-level risks — these identified misuse scenarios directly inform ISO 42001 A.9.2-4 design of safeguards, override mechanisms, and human oversight requirements for responsible AI use.
